title: Gravel Bike Geometry Project
text:
Current number of bike models in the database: 368!

A gravel bike finder tool
This site is designed to find the set of bikes that match the specifications you want in a frame. The focus is frame geometry, but there are also filters for material, suspension correction, UDH compatibility, sliding dropout, handlebar (flat or drop), axle spacing, and maximum tire width.
Two quick finder tools, with filters are:
A table of the classification of all gravel bike models in the database into Racy, Relaxed, and Rowdy categories.
A single plot that compares overall similarity of frame geometry among gravel bikes, color coded by style.


Gravel style
This site classifies bikes into Racy, Relaxed, and Rowdy styles based on their frame geometry.

Racy bikes are racy!
Relaxed bikes are relaxed!
Rowdy bikes are rowdy!

This is somewhat unique – most websites or podcasts that I know of categorize gravel bikes as “more racy” or “more mountain bikey”
Also…some hardtail mountain bikes are included because some hardtails make really good gravel bikes.


Which bikes are racy/relaxed/rowdy?
A table of the classification of all gravel bike models in the database into Racy, Relaxed, and Rowdy categories. This page has filters to view only bikes that match specific criteria, such as frame material or maximum tire width.
A single plot that compares overall similarity of frame geometry among gravel bikes, color coded by style. This page has filters to view only bikes that match specific criteria, such as frame material or maximum tire width.


What makes a racy frame racy? Or relaxed frame relaxed? Or rowdy frame rowdy?
What makes a racy frame racy?, a relaxed frame relaxed?, and a rowdy frame rowdy? - plots showing which frame measures are most correlated with a style, and which aren’t.


A gallery of frame measures
The Gravel 2D page contains interactive, 2D scatter plots of different pairs of frame geometry measures for all gravel bike models and frame sizes in the database.


How does my bike frame geometry change if I add suspension?
See how your bike frame’s geometry changes with a suspension fork.
See how your bike frame’s relative similarity to other bikes changes with a suspension fork.


A Tree Diagram of frame similarity
The Gravel Tree page contains a tree diagram showing the relative similarity in frame geometry among all gravel bikes in the database and the clustering of the models into three major styles.

title: Racy • Relaxed • Rowdy
text:
Current number of bike models in the database: 368!

I want a gravel bike for my local gravel races, or riding long days on unmaintained roads and trail, or underbiking singletrack. How do I begin?
Use these pages first

A table of the classification of all gravel bike models in the database into Racy, Relaxed, and Rowdy categories
A plot that compares overall similarity of frame geometry among gravel bikes.

These pages have filters for material, suspension correction, UDH compatibility, sliding dropout, handlebar (flat or drop), axle spacing, and maximum tire width.
Use the filters to narrow down the 368 models to the short list of bikes that check all the boxes.


Okay, what’s the next step?

A table to compare up to four bikes on key frame specs and frame geometry measures
Plots of specific frame measures for all gravel bike models and frame sizes in the database.



Sweet! Now I want to know what makes racy bikes racy, relaxed bikes relaxed, and rowdy bikes rowdy.
What makes Racy bikes racy!
What makes Relaxed bikes relaxed!
What makes Rowdy bikes rowdy!


What if I want to add suspension to the bikes on my shortlist?
First, make sure the manufacturer does not warn against a suspension fork. Then
See how your bike frame’s geometry changes with a suspension fork.
See how your bike frame’s relative similarity to other bikes changes with a suspension fork.

title: What makes a racy frame racy?
text:
Tip




Hover over data for model and frame size identification.
Scroll legend and click on items to identify specific model and frame size combinations.
Click on popup icon-bar over legend to zoom in/out and pan.









Note



Classification of gravel bikes is based on a frame size that fits a 175 cm high rider (generally frame size M or 54), according to manufacturer’s charts.



Racy bike frames have a combination of low stack, short front-center, high head tube angles, and low trail




















Racy frames have short reach, relative to rowdy frames








Racy frames have short chainstays (and rear-center), relative to relaxed frames








Racy frames can have low seat tube angles








Racy frames tend to have short front and rear centers. Relaxed frames tend to have long front and rear centers. So both racy and relaxed frames have low front-center:rear-center but for different reasons.








Stack:Reach and bottom brack drop aren’t really related to relaxedness

title: How does a suspension fork change bike geometry – Plots of data
text:
Tips for navigating




Hover over data for model and frame size identification.
Scroll legend and click on items to identify specific model.
Click on popup icon-bar over legend to zoom in/out and pan.









More notes!



More notes at the bottom!












Fork




rigid





30 mm





40 mm





50 mm














































Note



Classification of gravel bikes is based on a frame size that fits a 175 cm high rider (generally frame size M or 54), according to manufacturer’s charts.








Note



The suspension fork length and geometry is based on 20% sag: fork_length - 0.2*travel








A Rudy Fork geometry corrector



Rockshox recommends 5% sag on the Rudy fork while Fox, Cane Creek, and Lauf recommend (or are tuned for) 20% sag. The sus geometry for a 30 mm Rudy fork will be about 1/2 way between the 30 mm and 40 mm measures (for the same offset). The sus geometry for a 40 mm Rudy fork will be about 3/5 way between the 40 mm and 50 mm measures (for the same offset).








Is your frame suspension corrected?



Several companies are calling their frame suspension corrected, or sell a suspension fork with a build, but their rigid Axle-Crown length is far short (by > 10 mm and often > 15 mm) the sagged length of a 30 mm fork.








Gravel forks




Cane Creek Invert has two models: 30 mm (425 mm axle-crown) and 40 (435 mm axle-crown) mm travel. Both models have 45 mm offset
Rockshox Rudy has four models: 30 mm (425 mm axle-crown) and 40 (435 mm axle-crown) mm travel, each with either 45 mm or 51 mm offset.
Fox 32 TC Factory has four models: 40 (435.5 mm axle-crown) mm and 50 (445.5 mm axle-crown) mm travel, each with either 45 mm or 50 mm offset.
Lauf has one model with 30 mm travel (425 Axle Crown and 47 mm offset)

Stack, seattube angle, bottom bracket drop, and chainstay length aren’t really related to rowdiness

title: Gravel Tree
text:
Note




The tree was computed using Ward’s hierarchical clustering method.
The tree is based on a frame size that fits a 175 cm high rider (generally frame size M or 54), according to manufacturer’s charts. Splitting the tree into the three major clusters results in a classification that is close to, but not equivalent, to the classification computed using robust k-means (the classification elsewhere on this site).

title: A Gravel Bike Finder Tool
text:
This site is designed to find the set of bikes that match the specifications you want in a frame. The focus is frame geometry, but there are also filters for material, suspension correction, UDH compatibility, sliding dropout, handlebar (flat or drop), axle spacing, maximum tire width, cost, and more.
This site classifies gravel bikes into Racy, Relaxed, and Rowdy styles based on their frame geometry. This is somewhat unique – most websites or podcasts that I know of categorize gravel bikes as “more racy” or “more mountain bikey”
Also…some hardtail mountain bikes are included because some hardtails make really good gravel bikes.
